opinions.reason: Sec. 4 line 141 asserts the central architectural decision ('Two gates per commission, exactly two') is justified as sitting 'inside the inferred ceiling of one or two real gates per task' — but no citation, study, or anchor supports that ceiling anywhere in the document (I re-read the full paragraph and the surrounding Gate A/Gate B text; every other number in that section is footnoted, this one is not). This directly violates the artifact's own refusal rule in Sec. 3 ('No claim without an anchor; unanchored claims rejected unread') and its own R0 rung definition (Sec. 5: an unanchored claim is R0, not evidence) — the document fails the anchoring standard it imposes on the system it designs. This is a real internal-consistency defect in the argument for 'exactly two' gates, though the broader recommendation (git-committed state, substantiation-gated checker panel, refutation rungs) does not hinge solely on that phrase, so the central claim survives. Separately, per the default-refute-on-uncertainty instruction: the artifact was delivered truncated mid-sentence in Sec. 9 ('If exit-2 blocking is weaker than docum[ented]...') at exactly the point discussing the single most load-bearing risk to the whole enforcement mechanism (PreToolUse exit-2 always blocking), so I cannot verify how — or whether — that risk is resolved in the remaining ~9,000 uncited chars. I verified two of the artifact's other load-bearing citations (arxiv.org/html/2605.29800v1's rho-bar=0.391/n_eff=2.18 finding, and aclanthology.org/2023.findings-emnlp.467's 51.5%/74.5% figures) and both check out verbatim, so the sourcing discipline elsewhere is real — the gap at line 141 is the exception, not the norm, which is why I'm not calling it fatal.

Anchor failure in the #4 'runaway cost' bullet, artifact line 52 (grounding facts, first bullet after 'Ranked failure modes'). Two of the three concrete examples cited there have no supporting URL among the six sources the paragraph itself lists at its end (waxell dev.to, simonwillison.net, bytepro_1774 dev.to, pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/PMC10857587, cronitor.io, sjh9714 dev.to). I fetched dev.to/waxell/the-47000-agent-loop-...: it substantiates only the $47,000/11-day Analyzer<->Verifier case. I fetched dev.to/bytepro_1774/postmortem-preemption-split-a-multi-file-agent-apply-5568 in full: it is about process preemption during multi-file agent apply and contains no cost figures, no '$48,000', no '14 hours', no citation-finding task, and no call-count numbers at all. Neither of the other four listed sources (Supabase MCP writeup, HITL RCT PMC paper, Cronitor cron-dedup guide, 75.8%-self-graded dev.to post) is about cost or call counts either. So the '$48,000/14 hours from "find every citation supporting claim X"' figure and the '761 and 1,384 calls in 60 seconds from one idle-timeout bug' figure are both presented as grounded facts but are unanchored to any of the sources actually cited for that sentence -- exactly the failure mode (#10, 'unanchored claims') this artifact's own methodology exists to catch, and which it enforces on the maker ('no claim without an anchor; unanchored claims rejected unread', section 3) but fails to satisfy itself here. Both underlying facts do appear to be real (found via independent web search: the $48k/14hr case traces to an April 2026 research-agent postmortem, and the 761-1,384-calls-in-60s case traces to an openclaw/openclaw GitHub issue/PR thread) but the document cites neither of those actual sources, so as cited the claim does not check out. This does not overturn the central design conclusion (budget bounds are still justified by the properly-sourced $47k/11-day case alone), so severity is material, not fatal.

Ran live fetches against the three most load-bearing cited sources. cubic.dev/blog/does-pr-size-actually-matter: grep confirms the artifact's own withdrawal is correct — no '70-90%' or '~70% lower' string anywhere on the page (0 matches), while every figure the artifact says it re-grounded on IS present verbatim: '15% less likely to be reverted' (250 vs 50 lines), '75% of defects... one defect per 27 lines', 'Reviewer focus drops after 60 minutes', 'ideal PR size is under 200 lines'. survey.stackoverflow.co/2025/ai: 0 matches for '40%' anywhere on the page, confirming the artifact's own withdrawal of the 40%->29% trend claim; '46% actively distrust... 33%... trust' and '66%... almost right' both found verbatim, matching the artifact's replacement claims exactly. metr.org/blog/2025-07-10-early-2025-ai-experienced-os-dev-study: '19% longer', '20%... sped up... estimated', and '246 total' issues all confirmed verbatim. Every number I checked either matched exactly or matched the artifact's own disclosed self-correction in section 0 (which explicitly withdraws the two figures that don't check out and re-derives from what does). Per the disclosure rule, a gap the artifact itself names and resolves is not fatal. Did not re-verify every one of the ~40 other cited URLs/arXiv numbers (angle budget), but the pattern across the three highest-stakes empirical claims (the ones the artifact's own §0 flags as previously-refuted-and-corrected) is one of accurate, verbatim sourcing, not concealment or fabrication. No fatal defect found.
